options: A strong-looking relation between unrelated trending series
A regression with too few points
A regression with a negative slope
A regression of a stationary series on a season
why: Correct: the relation is a product of shared drift, not of a true link.
Few points give a different problem: high variance.
The sign of the slope has nothing to do with it.
A season is not the cause of a spurious result.

questions.q: Which pair of numbers is a warning sign for a spurious regression?
why: Correct: a high R² with a Durbin-Watson near 0 means the residuals are strongly autocorrelated.
Low R² and DW near 2 is a normal, uninteresting fit.
High R² with DW near 2 means the residuals look random. This is a good sign.
With R² of 0 there is no strong relation to explain.

questions.q: What is the usual first fix for a possible spurious regression?
options: Difference both series and use the changes
Take the square root of R²
why: Correct: changes of random walks are stationary, so the usual statistics are valid.
More variables do not fix non-stationary data.
This does not change anything about the data problem.
The test set size is not the issue.

questions.q: The cross-correlation corr(x(t), y(t+k)) is highest at k = 4. What does it mean?
options: x and y are the same series
why: Correct: x now matches y four steps later.
That would give a peak at k = -4.
Identical series give a peak at k = 0.
A peak above the band is a sign of a relation.

questions.q: Daily ad spend leads sales by 2 days (r = 0.6 at lag 2) and n = 100. The band is ±0.196. Is lag 2 significant?
options: No, because lag 2 is not zero
why: Correct: the band is 1.96/sqrt(100) = 0.196. A value of 0.6 is far outside.
1.96 is not the band. It is a z-value that is divided by sqrt(n).
n and the correlation are enough to compare with the band.
Lag does not need to be zero to be significant.

questions.q: A teammate finds a peak at lag 5 after checking 40 different lags and says it is a real effect. What is the main concern?
options: With 40 lags some bars are significant by chance (multiple testing)
A peak at lag 5 is never real
why: Correct: at a 5% level, about 2 of 40 lags look significant by chance. Check business logic and test on new data.
More lags would make the problem bigger.
A peak can be real. The point is to be careful.
Cross-correlation works at many lags.

questions.q: Two series both have a trend. You want to estimate their lead-lag link. What do you do first?
options: Compute the cross-correlation over a limited range of lags
Check the result with new data or a test
questions.why: Look first, then make the series stationary so trends do not create fake peaks, then compute the cross-correlation, then confirm on data that was not used to pick the lag.
